articles.title: NASA Administrator defends Learjet copilot after Florida crash
articles.summary: Jared Isaacman took to social media to defend the 20-year-old copilot of the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida on Nov. 1, killing all nine aboard.
articles.body:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman took to his personal social media account Nov. 2 to defend the female co-pilot of the Learjet that crashed near Palm Beach, Florida.

The private jet, bound from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, plummeted into the ground Nov. 1 near Greenacres and exploded into a fireball. All nine people onboard were killed.

The cause of the crash was not immediately known, but heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time the jet went down, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement.

Moments before the crash, a person in the cockpit said the crew was "managing the ice," encountering "moderate" turbulence and seeking "better rides," according to audio posted by LiveATC, a website that broadcasts air traffic control communications. That dramatic audio led to significant online criticism of the 20-year-old co-pilot, Nathalia Filgueiras, from Boca Raton. The pilot has not been identified.

"Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts," Isaacman wrote on X. "Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories. God bless them and their loved ones."

NASA Administrator defends Learjet copilot

"Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile strikes to DEI to critiquing this poor woman's final radio calls," Isaacman wrote.

Isaacman is an experienced jet pilot and commercial astronaut. He bankrolled and organized two orbital spaceflights with SpaceX. Both included women onboard, and his first, Inspiration4, featured a female pilot , Sian Proctor.

The NASA administrator went on to state that Filgueiras remained professional throughout the situation, knowing her life was about to end. She communicated with air traffic control right up until the crash.

"She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," he wrote.

"I understand the public interest given the footage and audio. But you do not know the aircraft's maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit," Isaacman wrote.

The leaked cockpit communication with air traffic control revealed that the crew saw ice and experienced turbulence before the crash occurred.

Isaacman said that it is common for charter companies, which fly these small jets, to hire fairly new commercial pilots and enable them to gain experience before many become commercial pilots. Filgueiras would have likely had all the applicable training, requirements, and checkouts required from the Federal Aviation Administration, he wrote.

Evidence suggests the aircraft began breaking apart before impact, National Transportation Safety Board member Thomas Chapman said at a Monday news conference.

Brooke Edwards is a Space Reporter for Florida Today. Contact her at bedwards@floridatoday.com or on X: @brookeofstars .

articles.title: Meet Ramya Manjunath Anche, the Bengaluru-born astronomer leading NASA's $20 million PUFFINS telescope mission to study tiny dust particles between stars
articles.summary: This is the story of Ramya Manjunath Anche, a Bengaluru-born astronomer preparing to study something that has remained difficult for scientists to
articles.body: This is the story of Ramya Manjunath Anche, a Bengaluru-born astronomer preparing to study something that has remained difficult for scientists to understand for decades. The subject is of the tiny particles of dust floating between stars. As a teenager fascinated by the 2003 Space Shuttle Columbia disaster, she has now grown up to lead a NASA-funded space telescope mission worth $20 million.Anche is now working as an assistant research professor at the University of Arizona’s Steward Observatory as the principal investigator of NASA’s PUFFINS mission. The aim of the mission is to investigate interstellar dust using a specialised ultraviolet telescope. The mission, selected under NASA’s Astrophysics Pioneers programme, received $20 million in funding in October 2026 and is targeted for launch in 2030.What makes her achievement interesting is that the scientist leading this ambitious international project began her journey in Devanahalli, a town near Bengaluru, India. She then went on to pursue engineering and astrophysics in India before taking her research career to the United States.Journey from a curious schoolgirl to an astronomerRamya Anche comes from a family where science was a regular subject of conversation. Her father, A Manjunath, is a microbiologist retired from the University of Agricultural Sciences in Bengaluru. His work in soil research at home helped nurture her curiosity from an early age.She attended Oxford English School in Devanahalli before studying at MES Vidyasagar Prof. MPL Sastry PU College in Bengaluru. She subsequently pursued a Bachelor of Engineering degree in electrical and electronics engineering from Sir M Visvesvaraya Institute of Technology.In an interview with The Indian Express, Anche said that she was always interested in research and that her family never pressured her to take up a conventional job.Space Shuttle Columbia disasterIt was the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster on February 1, 2003 that influenced her decision. The accident claimed the lives of seven astronauts and left a deep impression on her as a teenager and prompted her to wonder why the tragedy had happened. She went so deep that she wanted to understand whether it could have been prevented.The journey from electrical engineering to astrophysicsIn 2012, Anche joined the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru for an integrated MTech-PhD programme in astronomical instrumentation. Her academic journey subsequently took her to Pune, where she completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA) during 2020–21.In 2021, she moved to the United States. She was admitted to the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory and her work focuses on astronomical polarimetry, optical design, high-contrast imaging and the development of space telescopes.But one of the biggest milestones in her career came when she led a proposal for a NASA mission while still working as a postdoctoral researcher. The proposal eventually secured funding under NASA's Astrophysics Pioneers programme.What exactly is PUFFINS, the $20-million mission study?PUFFINS stands for Polarimetry in the Ultraviolet to Find Features in INterStellar Dust.These particles, known as interstellar dust grains, are incredibly small. As per the University of Arizona, PUFFINS will investigate grains smaller than approximately 50 nanometres, roughly the size of a common cold virus.Interstellar dust influences how light travels through space and is also connected to the formation of new stars and planets. Studying its composition, formation and behaviour can therefore help scientists understand how galaxies evolve and how the building blocks of planetary systems come together.To achieve this, PUFFINS will carry a specialised telescope measuring just 10 inches across, approximately the size of a large dinner plate. The mission will use a technique called ultraviolet spectropolarimetry.A team of 40 researchers and a 2030 launch targetAlthough Anche is leading the mission, PUFFINS is a collaboration of scientific efforts involving the University of Arizona, McDonald Observatory at the University of Texas at Austin and researchers from several institutions around the world.Around 40 scientists, engineers, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers are involved in the project. The team is currently in the early design phase, with the next four years expected to involve designing and building the telescope before its planned launch in 2030.

articles.title: A truck-sized NASA space telescope is about to crash to Earth
articles.summary: NASA’s Swift Observatory is now about to fall back to Earth on Wednesday after attempts to push it back into a higher orbit failed.﻿
articles.body: Almost 22 years after it was launched, NASA’s Swift Observatory is now about to fall back to Earth on Wednesday after attempts to push it back into a higher orbit failed. NASA announced that the aging space telescope is anticipated to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere at approximately 3:30AM ET (give or take 11 hours), and that it expects most of the spacecraft to burn up, but some components will likely survive re-entry. The observatory weighs around 3,200 pounds and measures in at 5.6 meters (18.4 feet) high and 5.4 meters (17.7 feet) wide, though much of the latter includes its deployable solar arrays. The risk of surviving components causing any harm is low, according to NASA: > “Re-entry locations of any surviving components can vary from hemisphere to hemisphere and depend on when it re-enters. Due to Swift’s low inclination, re-entry locations of surviving fragments are limited between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude. The risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely — approximately 1 in 2,100. NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions.” The agency gave up on trying to save the falling telescope earlier this year, after the Link spacecraft that was attempting the rescue experienced technical issues with attitude control. Still, Swift far outlived its original two-year prime mission to study the origin of gamma-ray bursts, and went on to serve as a general-purpose multi-wavelength observatory until solar storms pushed it into a lower orbit. You can follow Swift’s descent by monitoring NASA’s blog for continued updates.
